title: Navigation Math — TAS, Groundspeed, Headings, and Time/Distance/Fuel

required_knowledge_points.title: The Heading Sequence — TC → TH → MH → CH and 'East is Least'
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE will give a True Course and ask for the Compass Heading. Without knowing the four-step sequence and the East/West variation rule direction, the pilot calculates a heading that is off by twice the variation — the aircraft flies miles off course.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: The heading calculation sequence — never skipped, never reordered: (1) True Course (TC): course measured from True North on the chart. (2) True Heading (TH): TC ± Wind Correction Angle (WCA). If wind is from the left, crab right (add to TC). (3) Magnetic Heading (MH): TH ± Magnetic Variation. Rule: 'East is Least, West is Best.' East variation: SUBTRACT. West variation: ADD. Isogonic lines on sectional charts show variation. (4) Compass Heading (CH): MH ± Deviation. Deviation is caused by the aircraft's own magnetic field — correction card is mounted in the cockpit.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### The Heading Calculation Sequence — In Order, Never Skipped

| Step | From | To | Operation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Chart | **True Course (TC)** | Measured from **True North** on sectional chart |
| 2 | TC | **True Heading (TH)** | TC **± Wind Correction Angle (WCA)** |
| 3 | TH | **Magnetic Heading (MH)** | TH **± Magnetic Variation** |
| 4 | MH | **Compass Heading (CH)** | MH **± Compass Deviation** |

### Magnetic Variation — 'East is Least, West is Best'
- **East variation → SUBTRACT** from TH (makes MH smaller)
- **West variation → ADD** to TH (makes MH larger)
- Variation values found on **isogonic lines** on the sectional chart

### Compass Deviation
- Caused by the **aircraft's own magnetic field** — every aircraft is different
- Correction values found on the **compass correction card** mounted in the cockpit
- Apply to MH to get the final **Compass Heading (CH)** you actually fly

required_knowledge_points.title: TAS vs. IAS — Why Your Airspeed Indicator Lies at Altitude
required_knowledge_points.why: The most common navlog error: pilots use IAS for groundspeed calculations instead of TAS. At 8,000 feet, TAS can be 15% higher than IAS — producing an ETA that is significantly off and misleading fuel math.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Indicated Airspeed (IAS): what the airspeed indicator shows — the dynamic pressure of the airflow hitting the pitot tube. IAS does NOT equal actual aircraft speed through the air at altitude. True Airspeed (TAS): the actual speed of the aircraft moving through the surrounding air mass. TAS increases with altitude because at lower air density, the pitot tube senses less dynamic pressure for the same actual speed. Rule of thumb: TAS ≈ 2% higher per 1,000 feet of altitude. At 8,000 feet MSL with IAS 110 kts, TAS ≈ 128 kts. Groundspeed (GS) = TAS adjusted for wind. ETE = Distance ÷ GS — not IAS, not TAS.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Airspeed Types — Hierarchy

| Airspeed | What It Measures | Used For |
|---|---|---|
| **IAS** (Indicated) | Dynamic pressure on pitot tube | Aircraft performance limits (Vx, Vne, etc.) |
| **CAS** (Calibrated) | IAS corrected for instrument/position error | Intermediate step |
| **TAS** (True) | Actual speed through the surrounding air mass | Navlog calculation base |
| **GS** (Groundspeed) | TAS **adjusted for wind** | **ETE and ETA calculations** |

### TAS Rule of Thumb
- TAS increases approximately **2% per 1,000 feet** above sea level
- At **8,000 ft MSL**, IAS of 110 kts → TAS ≈ **128 kts**

### Navlog Math — Correct Sequence
1. Use **Winds Aloft** to determine wind vector at cruise altitude
2. Apply wind to TAS → compute **Groundspeed (GS)**
3. ETE = **Distance ÷ GS**

> Using IAS for ETE arrives early and creates fuel calculation errors — a navlog entry failure

required_knowledge_points.title: UTC Time Conversion and the Daylight Saving Trap
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE gives a departure time in local time and asks for the ETA in Zulu. The trap: in the summer, Eastern is UTC-4 (not -5). A pilot who always subtracts 5 from Eastern time will produce a Zulu ETA that is one hour off — a potential SAR trigger.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Aviation universally uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), also called Zulu time (Z). All METARs, TAFs, NOTAMs, and flight plan times are in UTC. Conversion offsets: Eastern Standard (EST) = UTC -5; Eastern Daylight (EDT) = UTC -4; Central Standard (CST) = UTC -6; Central Daylight (CDT) = UTC -5; Mountain Standard (MST) = UTC -7; Mountain Daylight (MDT) = UTC -6; Pacific Standard (PST) = UTC -8; Pacific Daylight (PDT) = UTC -7. To convert local to UTC: ADD the offset. To convert UTC to local: SUBTRACT the offset. Math trap: time is base 60 — ETE of 1.75 hours = 1 hour 45 minutes, NOT 1 hour 75 minutes.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### UTC / Zulu Time
- All aviation weather products, NOTAMs, and flight plans use **UTC (Coordinated Universal Time)** — also called **Zulu (Z)**

### US Time Zone Conversions
| Local Zone | Offset to UTC | Season |
|---|---|---|
| Eastern Standard (EST) | UTC **− 5** | Winter |
| Eastern Daylight (EDT) | UTC **− 4** | Summer |
| Central Standard (CST) | UTC **− 6** | Winter |
| Central Daylight (CDT) | UTC **− 5** | Summer |
| Mountain Standard (MST) | UTC **− 7** | Winter |
| Mountain Daylight (MDT) | UTC **− 6** | Summer |
| Pacific Standard (PST) | UTC **− 8** | Winter |
| Pacific Daylight (PDT) | UTC **− 7** | Summer |

**To convert Local → UTC:** ADD the offset value  
**To convert UTC → Local:** SUBTRACT the offset value

### Base-60 Math Trap
- ETE of **1.75 hours** = **1 hour 45 minutes** (NOT 1 hour 75 minutes)
- 0.5 hours = **30 minutes** (NOT 50 minutes)
- All ETE and UTC calculations use **base 60** — not base 100

required_knowledge_points.title: Fuel Requirements — The Legal Minimum vs. The Professional Standard
required_knowledge_points.why: The FAA's 30-minute day reserve is the legal floor, not the operational target. The DPE will present a scenario in which using the 30-minute minimum lands the pilot with zero margin. Additionally: fuel gauges are only legally required to be accurate at ZERO — using them alone for cross-country planning is unreliable.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: 14 CFR 91.151: VFR aircraft must carry enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing AND fly for at least 30 minutes more (day) or 45 minutes more (night) at normal cruising speed. The 30/45-minute reserve is the absolute minimum — professional standard is 1 hour. Fuel planning phases: (1) Startup/taxi/runup: use POH allowance (~1.0-1.5 gal). (2) Climb: use POH 'Time, Fuel, and Distance to Climb' chart. (3) Cruise: ETE × cruise GPH from POH power setting chart. (4) Reserve: cruise GPH × reserve time. Gauge unreliability: 14 CFR 23.1337 requires fuel gauges to be accurate ONLY at zero (empty). All positive readings are approximations — always physically measure with a calibrated dipstick at preflight.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Legal VFR Fuel Requirements (14 CFR 91.151)
| Operation | Required Reserve | Professional Standard |
|---|---|---|
| **Day VFR** | 30 minutes at cruise | 1 hour minimum |
| **Night VFR** | 45 minutes at cruise | 1 hour minimum |

### Four-Phase Fuel Planning (From POH)
1. **Startup/Taxi/Runup** — use POH allowance (~1.0–1.5 gallons)
2. **Climb** — use POH 'Time, Fuel, and Distance to Climb' chart
3. **Cruise** — ETE × cruise GPH (from POH power setting table at planned altitude)
4. **Reserve** — cruise GPH × reserve time (0.5 hr day min; use 1.0 hr professional standard)

### Fuel Gauge Limitation — 14 CFR 23.1337
- Fuel gauges are legally required to be accurate **only at zero (empty)**
- All positive gauge readings are **approximations only**
- **Always physically measure fuel** with a calibrated dipstick at preflight
- **Never use gauges alone** for cross-country fuel planning

lesson_overview:
## Navigation Math — The Numbers That Get You There and Back

A navlog is not bureaucratic paperwork. It is the pre-computed answer to every question the flight environment will ask you: What heading do I fly? When should I be at this checkpoint? How much fuel do I need to land with a legal reserve? The student who fills one out by rote passes the planning phase. The student who understands WHY each calculation works can update the answers in flight when conditions change.

**The heading sequence: TC to CH, four steps, never skipped.** Dead reckoning navigation follows a locked four-step sequence. True Course — drawn on the sectional and measured from True North. True Heading — add or subtract the Wind Correction Angle from the Winds Aloft forecast (if wind is from the left, crab right by adding to TC). Magnetic Heading — apply magnetic variation from the isogonic lines on the sectional using the 'East is Least, West is Best' rule. Compass Heading — apply the deviation correction from the correction card mounted in the aircraft's cockpit. The most common student error: applying variation in the wrong direction. The result is a heading error of twice the variation compounding over the full flight.

**TAS vs. IAS: why the airspeed indicator lies at altitude.** The airspeed indicator measures dynamic pressure — the ram-air pressure on the pitot tube. At sea level, IAS closely matches TAS. At altitude, the air is thinner — less dynamic pressure for the same actual speed. The instrument under-reads. At 8,000 feet, TAS is approximately 16% higher than IAS. The critical navlog error: using IAS as the groundspeed input. Groundspeed = TAS ± wind. ETE = Distance ÷ Groundspeed. Using IAS produces an ETE that is too long and an ETA that is systematically off.

**UTC and the daylight saving trap.** All aviation weather, flight plans, and NOTAMs use UTC (Zulu time). Eastern Standard Time is UTC minus 5. Eastern Daylight Time (summer) is UTC minus 4. Students who always subtract 5 from Eastern time are one hour off during Daylight Saving months — producing an ETA that is wrong by 60 minutes and potentially triggering a search and rescue sequence if a flight plan was filed. Time calculations are also base-60: 1.75 hours is 1 hour and 45 minutes, not 1 hour and 75 minutes.

**Fuel planning: the 30-minute reserve is a floor, not a target.** 14 CFR 91.151 requires day VFR aircraft to carry enough fuel to reach the destination plus 30 minutes at cruise. Night VFR: 45 minutes. The professional planning target is one hour of reserve minimum. Fuel quantity gauges are only legally required to be accurate at zero — every positive reading is an approximation. Physical dipstick measurement at preflight is the only reliable source for fuel quantity before a cross-country.

**The checkride trap:** The DPE hands you an E6B and a segment of the navlog. The checks: do you use IAS or TAS for groundspeed? Do you apply variation in the right direction? Do you add or subtract WCA correctly? Do you convert ETE to UTC correctly for the local time zone — including checking DST? All four are individually testable on one short segment.
